introduction-proactive-vs-reactive-finop.core: Reactive FinOps fixes bills after they arrive. Proactive (architectural) FinOps designs cost in from the start, choosing storage tiers, data flows and topology so the system is cheap by construction.

first_principles.problem: Expensive architectural decisions (cross-region chatter, everything in hot storage) are locked in, and a refactor later costs far more than designing it right.
truths: Architecture determines most of the cost.
Changing an architecture later is expensive.
Cost can be a design requirement.

analogy.title: Insulating a house while building vs. after
analogy.story: Insulation during construction is cheap; retrofitting means tearing down walls.
analogy.breaks: Over-optimising early can slow delivery, so focus on the big cost drivers.

example.title: A design review with a cost estimate

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Savings designed in before a line of code is written.

example.outcome: systems that are cheap by construction.

check.q: Why is proactive FinOps cheaper than reactive?
check.a: Changing an architecture after it's built is far more expensive than designing for cost up front.

tiered-storage-economics.core: Storage classes trade access cost and latency against price per GB: hot (S3 Standard), warm (Infrequent Access), cold (Glacier Instant/Flexible) and archive (Deep Archive). Match each dataset's access temperature to its tier.

first_principles.problem: Petabytes of rarely read logs sit in Standard storage at up to 20x the archive price.
truths: Access frequency drops as data ages.
Cheaper tiers charge more to retrieve.

analogy.title: Kitchen counter, pantry, basement and off-site storage
analogy.story: Daily items on the counter, holiday decorations in the attic, old tax records in off-site storage.
analogy.breaks: Retrieval and request fees can make cold tiers more expensive for data that turns out to be read often.

check.q: What's the main trade-off of colder storage tiers?
check.a: Lower per-GB price in exchange for higher retrieval cost, slower access and minimum storage durations.

s3-lifecycle-policies-automating-tier-tr.core: Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects to colder tiers by age (and prefix or tag), and expire them when no longer needed, so data temperature management is hands-off.

first_principles.problem: Manually moving objects between tiers doesn't scale, so nobody does it and costs climb.
truths: Age is a strong proxy for access frequency.
Rules apply to billions of objects automatically.
derivation: **Transition**: Standard → IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90.
Clean up **noncurrent versions** and **incomplete multipart uploads**.

analogy.title: An automatic filing system
analogy.story: Papers move from desk to cabinet to archive box on a schedule, and are shredded after 7 years.
analogy.breaks: Transitioning many tiny objects can cost more than it saves because of per-object fees.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Logs flow to cheaper tiers automatically and disappear after 7 years.

check.a: Failed multipart uploads leave invisible parts that keep incurring storage charges.

data-transfer-topology-the-hidden-tollbo.core: Clouds charge per GB to move data across AZs, across regions, out to the internet and through NAT gateways. Topology decisions (where services, caches and data sit) can quietly dominate the bill.

first_principles.problem: A chatty microservice architecture spread across AZs, with traffic routed through NAT, generates a larger transfer bill than its compute bill.
truths: Cross-AZ, cross-region and egress cost money.
NAT gateways charge per GB processed.
derivation: Keep chatty services **in the same AZ** (topology-aware routing).
Use **VPC endpoints** for AWS services instead of NAT.

analogy.title: Toll roads between towns
analogy.story: Driving within town is free; every trip between towns costs a toll, so you plan routes to minimise crossings.
analogy.breaks: Keeping everything in one AZ reduces resilience, so balance cost against availability.

example.title: NAT gateway surprise
flow: Pods pull from S3 via NAT: 200 TB/mo

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One routing change saves $100k a year.

example.outcome: network costs are designed, not discovered.

check.q: Why route S3 traffic through a VPC gateway endpoint instead of NAT?
check.a: Gateway endpoints for S3 are free, while NAT charges per GB processed.
